rules: R1: only the kanji in pipeline/jp/kanji_n5_n4.json (the Tanos JLPT N5 and N4 lists, plus its recorded operator additions), else the whole word in hiragana
R2: words normally written in hiragana stay in hiragana
R4: one bracket per kanji word, okurigana outside
R5: the kanji matches the meaning in context
R6: a common word whose kanji are all in kanji_n5_n4.json is not left in hiragana
R7: a choose item writes its options alike
R8: the pronoun わたし is written 私{わたし} (Mark's ruling of 2026-10-26)
R9: わかる is written 分{わ}かる, 分 being a recorded operator addition (Mark's ruling of 2026-10-26)
method: publish.check_draft checked every reading. The drafter's own review pass and a separate LM judge session that did not write the twins then read every twin in context. Each finding names the twin by point, item (ex<N> example or p<N> practice), field and list index. After the judge pass, a re-audit read every twin that carries a homophone-class kanji (書 or 描, 買 or 勝, 行 or 言, 早 or 速, 開 or 空, 止 or 泊, 着 or 付, 借 or 貸, 送 or 贈, 切 or 着) against its English gloss, in place of a second judge session. Its findings carry by: re-audit. The first scripted kanji pass had no committed list. On 2026-10-26 Mark ruled the list strict: review/apply_kanji_rulings.py rewrote every twin against the committed pipeline/jp/kanji_n5_n4.json (R1) and wrote わたし as 私{わたし} (R8). A later ruling the same day added 分 as an operator addition, and the same script wrote every form of わかる as 分{わ}かる (R9). Those findings carry by: operator-ruling, and test_kanji_list.py checks every twin's kanji against the file.
